summary:
Psalms is ancient Israel's book of prayers and songs: 150 poems addressed to God. "Psalm" comes from the Greek psalmos, a song sung to strings; the Hebrew title is Tehillim, "praises." Titles above most psalms name their sources: seventy-three say "of David"; others name Asaph and the sons of Korah, Levitical families of temple singers (1 Chronicles 25:1); two name Solomon; and Psalm 90 is headed "A prayer of Moses the man of God." And Psalm 137 opens, "By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion" — the exile of 586 BC — so the collection was still growing at least four centuries after David.

The poems are arranged in five books (1–41; 42–72; 73–89; 90–106; 107–150), a division marked in the text and compared in Jewish tradition to the five books of Moses. Each of the first four books ends with a doxology, a closing formula of blessing: "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen" (41:13; 72:18–19; 89:52; 106:48). Book Two even signs off, "Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse" (72:20), though more "of David" psalms follow. Two untitled psalms form the doorway: Psalm 1 sets out the two ways, blessing "the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked," and Psalm 2 presents the LORD's "Anointed One" — Hebrew mashiach, the word behind "Messiah."

Most psalms fall into recognizable kinds. Laments — prayers from trouble that complain and plead, usually turning back to trust — are commonly counted the largest group; Psalm 22 begins with the cry Jesus prayed from the cross, "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46), and Psalm 88, often called the darkest in the book, ends "darkness is my closest companion." Alongside them are hymns of praise, thanksgivings for rescue, psalms of trust like Psalm 23 ("The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want"), royal psalms for the king (2; 110), wisdom psalms (1; 73), and the fifteen Songs of Ascents (120–134), each titled "A song of ascents," usually taken as pilgrim songs for festival journeys up to Jerusalem. A few curse: Psalm 137 ends by blessing the one who repays Babylon by dashing its infants against the rocks — the imprecatory (curse) psalms.

Hebrew poetry rhymes ideas rather than sounds. Its device is parallelism: a line speaks, and the next repeats it in different words, sharpens it, or turns it around. "Praise the LORD, all you nations! Extol Him, all you peoples!" — those lines open Psalm 117, which at two verses is the shortest chapter in the Bible. Psalm 119, a poem in praise of God's law, is the longest at 176 verses: an acrostic working through the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, eight verses per letter. Many titles carry performance notes — "For the choirmaster," even a tune: Psalm 22 is sung "To the tune of 'The Doe of the Dawn'" — and the word Selah appears seventy-one times; its meaning is uncertain, probably a musical pause.

The New Testament quotes Psalms constantly. Psalm 110:1 — "Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet" — is often counted the Old Testament verse the New Testament cites most (Matthew 22:44; Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13), and Psalm 118:22, "The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone," is applied to Jesus in Matthew 21:42, Acts 4:11, and 1 Peter 2:7. Laments cluster early and praise dominates the end — often described as the book's arc from lament to praise. The close is five psalms, 146–150, each opening and closing with "Hallelujah!" — Hebrew for "praise the LORD" — the last of them summoning horn, harp, lyre, tambourine, dancing, strings, flute, and cymbals to the final line: "Let everything that has breath praise the LORD! Hallelujah!" (150:6).
